'''Joos Ulrich Heintz''' (27 October 1945 - 3 October 2024) was an Argentinean-Swiss mathematician. He was a professor [[emeritus]] at the [[University of Buenos Aires]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.uba.ar/archivos_uba/2014-09-10_968.pdf|title=Resolution University of Buenos Aires EXP-UBA 36.186/2014}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Heintz was born on 27 October 1945 in [[Zürich]], Switzerland. After studying Mathematics and [[Cultural anthropology|Cultural Anthropology]] at the [[University of Zurich]] to undergraduate level, he went on to receive a PhD in mathematics in 1982 under the supervision of [[Volker Strassen]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=44666|title=Joos Ulrich Heintz at the Mathematics Genealogy Project}}</ref> He performed his [[habilitation]] in 1986 at the [[Goethe University Frankfurt|J.W.von Goethe University]] in [[Frankfurt|Frankfurt am Main]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.uni-frankfurt.de/50699934/entwu_pc.pdf|title=W. Schwarz, J. Wolfart. Zur Geschichte des Mathematischen Seminars der Universität Frankfurt am Main von 1914 bis 1970 (2002)}}</ref> where he also studied [[Turkology|Turcology]] and Sephardic history and culture. He was appointed [[Privatdozent]] at the J.W. Goethe university Frankfurt am Main. Until his retirement in 2017, he worked as a Full Professor at the University of Buenos Aires and [[University of Cantabria]]/Spain and as a Senior Researcher at the [[National Council for Scientific and Technological Development|National Council for Scientific and Technological Development (CONICET)]].

== Research ==
Heintz worked mainly in algebraic complexity theory, computational algebraic geometry, and semi algebraic geometry. For this purpose, he developed with his collaborators, different mathematical tools, e.g. the Bezout Inequality<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Heintz|first=Joos|date=1983|title=Definability and fast quantifier elimination in algebraically closed fields|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=24|issue=3|pages=239–277|doi=10.1016/0304-3975(83)90002-6|doi-access=free}}</ref> or the first effective [[Nullstellensatz]] in arbitrary characteristic.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Caniglia|first1=L.|last2=Heintz|first2=J.|last3=Galligo|first3=A.|date=1988|title=Borne simple exponentielle pour les degrés dans le théorème des zéros sur un corps de caractéristique quelconque|journal=Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|volume=307|pages=255–258}}</ref> This allowed him and his collaborators to adapt Kronecker's elimination theory<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kronecker|first=Leopold|date=1882|title=Grundzüge einer algebraischen Theorie der arithmetischen Grössen|journal=Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik|volume=92|pages=1–122}}</ref> to the complexity requirements of modern [[computer algebra]] and to prove that all reasonable geometric (not algebraic) computation problems are solvable in [[PSPACE]]. Later, he extended these complexity results to polynomial input systems given by arithmetic circuits. The outcome was a worst case optimal probabilistic elimination algorithm with the ability to recognize “easily solvable” input systems which was later implemented by Grégoire Lecerf.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Giusti|first1=M.|last2=Lecerf|first2=G.|last3=Salvy|first3=B.|date=2001|title=A Gröbner free alternative for polynomial system solving|journal=Journal of Complexity|volume=17|pages=154–211|doi=10.1006/jcom.2000.0571|doi-access=free}}</ref> Finally, Heintz and his collaborators demonstrated that under fragile and natural assumptions, the worst case complexity of elimination algorithms is unavoidably exponential, independent of the chosen data structure.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bank|first1=B.|last2=Heintz|first2=Joos|last3=Matera|first3=G.|last4=Montaña|first4=J.L.|last5=Pardo|first5=L.M.|last6=Rojas Paredes|first6=A.|date=2016|title=Quiz games as a model for information hiding|journal=Journal of Complexity|volume=34|pages=1–29|doi=10.1016/j.jco.2015.11.005|arxiv=1508.07842|s2cid=31037127 }}</ref> He applied his results and methods also to mixed integer optimization<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bank|first1=B.|last2=Heintz|first2=J.|last3=Krick|first3=T.|last4=Mandel|first4=R.|last5=Solernó|first5=P.|date=1993|title=Une borne optimale pour la programmation entière quasi-convexe|journal=Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France|volume=121|issue=2|pages=299–314|doi=10.24033/bsmf.2210|doi-access=free}}</ref> and foundations of [[software engineering]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Heintz|first1=J.|last2=Kuijpers|first2=B.|last3=Rojas Paredes|first3=A.|date=2013|title=Software Engineering and complexity in effective Algebraic Geometry|journal=Journal of Complexity|volume=29|pages=92–138|doi=10.1016/j.jco.2012.04.005|doi-access=free|arxiv=1110.3030}}</ref>

Furthermore, in the field of linguistics, he identified the [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]] and [[phonology]] of the Turkish languages as a regular language.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Heintz|first1=Joos|last2=Schönig|first2=Claus|date=1991|title=Turkic morphology as regular language|url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/41927774|journal=Central Asiatic Journal|volume=35|issue=1–2|pages=96–122|jstor=41927774 }}</ref>

In 1987, Heintz founded the Argentinean research group [[Noaï Fitchas]] in Buenos Aires. This group was transformed into the international working group [[TERA (Turbo Evaluation and Rapid Algorithms)]] with collaborators from several Argentinean, French, Spanish and German universities and research institutions, such as the University of Buenos Aires, CONICET, [[University of Nice Sophia Antipolis|University of Nice]], École Polytechnique at Paris, [[University of Cantabria|Universidad de Cantabria]] (Spain), and [[Humboldt University of Berlin|Humboldt University]] at Berlin. Noaï Fitchas was used as a pseudonym for the Argentinean group and numerous influential papers in Computer Algebra were published in the nineties under this name.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Berenstein|first1=C.A.|last2=Struppa|first2=D.C.|date=1991|title=Recent improvements in the complexity of the effective Nullstellensatz|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=157|pages=203–215|doi=10.1016/0024-3795(91)90115-D|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Heintz|first=Joos|year=2021|title=La complejidad es el momento de la verdad|url=https://aargentinapciencias.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/03-RESENA-Heintz-CeIResenasT9N2-2021indd.pdf|journal=Ciencia e Investigacion. Reseñas|publisher=Asociación Argentina para el Progreso de las Ciencias|volume=9|issue=2|pages=43–55}}</ref>

Heintz was a member of the editorial boards of several international journals, including the Foundations of Computational Mathematics, Computational Complexity and Applicable Algebra in Engineering, and Communication and Computing, from which he received three best paper awards.

In 2003, Heintz was awarded the Argentinean [[Konex Award|Konex Medal of Merit]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fundacionkonex.org/b2570-joos-yunus-heintz|title=Premio Konex 2003: Ingeniería Electrónica, Comunicación e Informática}}</ref>

* Caniglia L., Galligo A., Heintz J. (1989) Some new effectivity bounds in computational geometry. In: Mora T. (eds) Applied Algebra, Algebraic Algorithms and Error-Correcting Codes. AAECC 1988. * Bank B, Giusti M., Heintz J.,  Mbakop G.M. (1997). Polar varieties, real equation solving, and data structures: the hypersurface case. Journal of Complexity 13 (1). pp.&nbsp;5–27 https://doi.org/10.1006/jcom.1997.0432 1997 Journal of Complexity Best Paper Award
* Giusti M., Heintz J., Morais J.E., Morgenstern J., Pardo L.M. (1998). Straight-line programs in geometric elimination theory. [[Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra]] 124 (1-3) (1998) 101-146 https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-4049(96)00099-0
* Heintz J., Kuijpers B., Rojas Paredes A. (2013). Software Engineering and complexity in effective Algebraic Geometry. Journal of Complexity 29 (1). pp.&nbsp;92–138 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jco.2012.04.005 2013 Journal of Complexity Best Paper Award
* Bank B., Giusti M., Heintz J., Lecerf G., Matera G., Solernó G. (2015). Degeneracy Loci and Polynomial Equation Solving. [[Foundations of Computational Mathematics]], 15 (1). pp.&nbsp;159–184 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-014-9214-z
